Specifically, smoothness of the input is rarely discussed, even though it is a critical property to define the character of the solutions and the validity of the methods and formulas prescribed. On the other hand, the relationships with the state space representation (SSR) of linear systems is absent from this same literature and only marginally discussed in more advanced texts. In this paper we detail these gaps left behind in the didactic literature, then we provide a formal delimitation of the boundaries of the standard solutions and methods for linear ODE's. Our analysis relies on some key properties of state space representations, so we establish the formal connections between ODEs and SSR's, defining an equivalence between the two that is absent in the literature and is of conceptual interest by itself.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies gaps in didactic literature regarding ODE solution methods, particularly concerning input smoothness assumptions and connections to state space representations, and provides formal boundaries for linear ODE solutions while establishing equivalence between ODEs and SSRs.
AI.motivation: Standard didactic literature on ODEs in engineering education lacks clarity about assumptions behind solution methods, particularly regarding input smoothness requirements and connections to state space representations, creating gaps in understanding applicability limits.
AI.method: Analyzes gaps in existing literature, provides formal delimitation of boundaries for standard linear ODE solutions, and establishes equivalence between ODEs and state space representations using key properties of SSRs.
AI.result: Provides formal boundaries for standard solution methods of linear ODEs, clarifies assumptions about input smoothness, and establishes formal equivalence between ODEs and state space representations that is absent in existing literature.
AI.conclusion: The paper fills important gaps in didactic literature by clarifying assumptions behind ODE solution methods, establishing formal boundaries for their applicability, and providing conceptual equivalence between ODEs and state space representations that enhances understanding of linear systems theory.

title: From Cut-In to Rated: Multi-Region Floating Offshore Wind Farm Control for Secondary Frequency Regulation
summary: This paper describes a multi-region control framework for floating offshore wind farms. Specifically, we propose a novel generator torque controller that regulates rotor speed in Region 2, corresponding to wind speeds between the cut-in and rated values. In Region 3 (wind speeds at or above rated but below cut-out speed) we employ a PI-LQR for collective blade pitch. Control blending across the transitional wind speeds (Region 2.5) employs a sigmoid weighting function applied to the control variables. Two modeling paradigms are proposed for farm-level power tracking with rotor speed regularization: a nonlinear model predictive controller (NL-MPC) with a dynamic wake model, and a reduced order model predictive controller based on linear parameter varying turbine models with a time delay representation of wake advection (LPVTD-MPC). These approaches are evaluated over three wind inlet conditions using the PJM ancillary service certification criteria for participation in a secondary frequency regulation market. Results show that both approaches achieve scores of at least 89.9\% for the three different testing scenarios, which are well above the qualification threshold of 75\%. However, the LPVTD-MPC approach solves the problem in under half the time versus NL-MPC but with slightly larger fluctuations in farm-level power output, highlighting the trade-off between performance and computational tractability. The control framework is among the first to address multi-region wind turbine dynamics together with market driven power tracking objectives for floating offshore wind farms. Such multi-region control becomes increasingly necessary in the floating turbine setting where large (region spanning) wind speed variations are common due to wave induced platform pitching.

AI.tldr: A multi-region control framework for floating offshore wind farms with novel torque control in Region 2, PI-LQR for pitch in Region 3, sigmoid blending in Region 2.5, and two MPC approaches (NL-MPC and LPVTD-MPC) for farm-level power tracking with rotor speed regularization, evaluated using PJM ancillary service criteria.
AI.motivation: Floating offshore wind farms experience large wind speed variations due to wave-induced platform pitching, necessitating multi-region control that addresses turbine dynamics across different operational regions while meeting market-driven power tracking objectives for participation in frequency regulation markets.
AI.method: 1) Novel generator torque controller for Region 2 (cut-in to rated wind speeds); 2) PI-LQR for collective blade pitch in Region 3 (rated to cut-out wind speeds); 3) Sigmoid weighting function for control blending in transitional Region 2.5; 4) Two MPC approaches: nonlinear MPC with dynamic wake model (NL-MPC) and reduced-order linear parameter varying turbine models with time delay wake advection (LPVTD-MPC) for farm-level power tracking with rotor speed regularization.
AI.result: Both MPC approaches achieved scores ≥89.9% across three wind inlet conditions using PJM ancillary service certification criteria, well above the 75% qualification threshold. LPVTD-MPC solved the problem in under half the time of NL-MPC but with slightly larger fluctuations in farm-level power output, demonstrating a performance-computation trade-off.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-region control framework successfully addresses floating offshore wind farm dynamics across operational regions while meeting market-driven power tracking objectives. The LPVTD-MPC offers computational advantages with acceptable performance trade-offs, making it suitable for real-time applications. This represents one of the first frameworks to integrate multi-region turbine control with market participation objectives for floating offshore wind farms.

title: Bandwidth reduction methods for packetized MPC over lossy networks
comment: Accepted at the European Control Conference 2026; 8 pages; 5 figures
summary: We study the design of an offloaded model predictive control (MPC) operating over a lossy communication channel. We introduce a controller design that utilizes two complementary bandwidth-reduction methods. The first method is a multi-horizon MPC formulation that decreases the number of optimization variables, and therefore the size of transmitted input trajectories. The second method is a communication-rate reduction mechanism that lowers the frequency of packet transmissions. We derive theoretical guarantees on recursive feasibility and constraint satisfaction under minimal assumptions on packet loss, and we establish reference-tracking performance for the rate-reduction strategy. The proposed methods are validated using a hardware-in-the-loop setup with a real 5G network, demonstrating simultaneous improvements in bandwidth efficiency and computational load.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a bandwidth-efficient offloaded MPC design using multi-horizon formulation and communication-rate reduction for lossy channels, with theoretical guarantees and 5G hardware validation.
AI.motivation: To address bandwidth limitations and packet loss in offloaded MPC systems operating over lossy communication channels, particularly for applications requiring efficient bandwidth utilization and reliable control performance.
AI.method: Two complementary bandwidth-reduction methods: 1) multi-horizon MPC formulation that reduces optimization variables and transmitted input trajectory size, and 2) communication-rate reduction mechanism that lowers packet transmission frequency.
AI.result: Theoretical guarantees for recursive feasibility and constraint satisfaction under minimal packet loss assumptions, plus reference-tracking performance for rate-reduction strategy. Hardware-in-the-loop validation with real 5G network shows simultaneous improvements in bandwidth efficiency and computational load.
AI.conclusion: The proposed dual-method approach effectively addresses bandwidth constraints in offloaded MPC systems while maintaining control performance, with practical validation demonstrating feasibility in real-world 5G network environments.

title: Stability and Sensitivity Analysis for Objective Misspecifications Among Model Predictive Game Controllers
summary: Model-based multi-agent control requires agents to possess a model of the behavior of others to make strategic decisions. Solution concepts from game theory are often used to model the emergent collective behavior of self-interested agents and have found active use in multi-agent control design. Model predictive games are a class of controllers in which an agent iteratively solves a finite-horizon game to predict the behavior of a multi-agent system and synthesize their own control action. When multiple agents implement these types of controllers, there may exist misspecifications in the respective game models embedded in their controllers, stemming from inaccurate estimates or conjectures of other agents' objectives. This paper analyzes the resulting prediction misalignments and their effects on the system's behavior. We provide criteria for the stability of multi-agent dynamic systems with heterogeneous model predictive game controllers, and quantify the sensitivity of the equilibria to individual agents' game parameters.

AI.tldr: Analysis of stability and sensitivity in multi-agent systems with model predictive game controllers when agents have misspecified models of others' objectives.
AI.motivation: Model predictive games require agents to have accurate models of others' behavior, but in practice agents often have misspecified models due to inaccurate estimates or conjectures about others' objectives. This leads to prediction misalignments that affect system behavior.
AI.method: The paper analyzes prediction misalignments in multi-agent systems with heterogeneous model predictive game controllers. It provides stability criteria for such systems and quantifies the sensitivity of equilibria to individual agents' game parameters.
AI.result: The paper establishes stability criteria for multi-agent dynamic systems with model predictive game controllers and quantifies how equilibria are affected by agents' game parameter misspecifications.
AI.conclusion: Understanding and quantifying the effects of model misspecifications in model predictive game controllers is crucial for designing robust multi-agent control systems, as these misspecifications lead to prediction misalignments that impact system stability and equilibrium behavior.

title: Bayesian Inference for Estimating Generation Costs in Electricity Markets
summary: Estimating generation costs from observed electricity market data is essential for market simulation, strategic bidding, and system planning. To that end, we model the relationship between generation costs and production schedules with a latent variable model. Estimating generation costs from observed schedules is then formulated as Bayesian inference. A prior distribution encodes an initial belief on parameters, and the inference consists of updating the belief with the posterior distribution given observations. We use balanced neural posterior estimation (BNPE) to learn this posterior. Validation on the IEEE RTS-96 test system shows that marginal costs are recovered with narrow credible intervals, while start-up costs remain largely unidentifiable from schedules alone. The method is benchmarked against an inverse-optimization algorithm that exhibits larger parameter errors without uncertainty quantification.

AI.tldr: BNPE enables Bayesian inference of generation costs from market data with uncertainty quantification, outperforming inverse optimization.
AI.motivation: Estimating generation costs from observed electricity market data is crucial for market simulation, strategic bidding, and system planning, but existing methods lack proper uncertainty quantification.
AI.method: Formulate cost estimation as Bayesian inference using a latent variable model, employ balanced neural posterior estimation (BNPE) to learn posterior distributions, and validate on IEEE RTS-96 test system.
AI.result: BNPE recovers marginal costs with narrow credible intervals but start-up costs remain largely unidentifiable from schedules alone; outperforms inverse-optimization algorithm which has larger parameter errors without uncertainty quantification.
AI.conclusion: BNPE provides a robust Bayesian framework for cost estimation with uncertainty quantification, though start-up cost identifiability requires additional information beyond production schedules.

title: Data-Driven Moving Horizon Estimators for Linear Systems with Sample Complexity Analysis
summary: This paper investigates the state estimation problem for linear systems subject to Gaussian noise, where the model parameters are unknown. By formulating and solving an optimization problem that incorporates both offline and online system data, a novel data-driven moving horizon estimator (DDMHE) is designed. We prove that the expected 2-norm of the estimation error of the proposed DDMHE is ultimately bounded. Further, we establish an explicit relationship between the system noise covariances and the estimation error of the proposed DDMHE. Moreover, through a sample complexity analysis, we show how the length of the offline data affects the estimation error of the proposed DDMHE. We also quantify the performance gap between the proposed DDMHE using noisy data and the traditional moving horizon estimator with known system matrices. Finally, the theoretical results are validated through numerical simulations.

AI.tldr: A novel data-driven moving horizon estimator (DDMHE) is developed for linear systems with unknown parameters and Gaussian noise, using both offline and online data to achieve ultimately bounded estimation error.
AI.motivation: Traditional moving horizon estimators require known system matrices, but in practice, model parameters are often unknown. There's a need for state estimation methods that can handle unknown system parameters while maintaining performance guarantees.
AI.method: Formulates and solves an optimization problem incorporating both offline and online system data to design a data-driven moving horizon estimator (DDMHE). The approach combines data-driven learning with moving horizon estimation principles.
AI.result: Proves the expected 2-norm of estimation error is ultimately bounded, establishes explicit relationship between noise covariances and estimation error, analyzes sample complexity showing how offline data length affects error, and quantifies performance gap between DDMHE and traditional MHE with known matrices.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DDMHE effectively addresses state estimation for linear systems with unknown parameters, providing theoretical guarantees and validated performance through numerical simulations, bridging the gap between data-driven methods and traditional model-based estimation.

title: Data-Driven Power Flow for Radial Distribution Networks with Sparse Real-Time Data
summary: Real-time control of distribution networks requires accurate information about the system state. In practice, however, such information is difficult to obtain because real-time measurements are available only at a limited number of locations. This paper proposes a novel data-driven power flow (DDPF) framework for balanced radial distribution networks. The proposed algorithm combines the behavioral approach with the DistFlow model and leverages offline historical data to solve power flow problems using only a limited set of real-time measurements. To design DDPF under sparse measurement conditions, we develop a sensor placement problem based on optimal network reductions. This allows us to determine sensor locations subject to a predefined sensor budget and to explicitly account for the radial nature of distribution networks. Unlike approaches that rely on full observability, the proposed framework is designed for practical distribution grids with sparse measurement availability. This enables data-driven power flow for real-time operation while reducing the number of required sensors. On several test cases, the proposed DDPF algorithm could demonstrate accurate voltage magnitude predictions, with a maximum error less than 0.001 p.u., with as little as 25% of total locations equipped with sensors.

AI.tldr: A data-driven power flow framework for radial distribution networks that uses historical data and sparse real-time measurements to achieve accurate voltage predictions with only 25% sensor coverage.
AI.motivation: Real-time control of distribution networks requires accurate system state information, but this is difficult to obtain due to limited real-time measurements available at only a few locations in practical distribution grids.
AI.method: Proposes a novel data-driven power flow (DDPF) framework combining behavioral approach with DistFlow model, leveraging offline historical data. Develops a sensor placement problem based on optimal network reductions to determine sensor locations subject to budget constraints while accounting for radial network structure.
AI.result: The DDPF algorithm demonstrated accurate voltage magnitude predictions with maximum error less than 0.001 p.u. using only 25% of total locations equipped with sensors across several test cases.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables data-driven power flow for real-time operation in practical distribution grids with sparse measurement availability, reducing sensor requirements while maintaining accuracy.
